subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
Lavanya, sit down, I'll tell you why I never forward anything the moment it arrives. I'm Aparna, and I was a young woman of twenty-four, waiting at the bus stop across from Bhaskar's stationery shop. A voice note was going round the phones: a child had been taken from that shop. Within minutes forty people stood outside, shouting, some pushing at the shutter. Bhaskar stood behind his counter, pale, hands raised, unable to speak.

I couldn't say what was true. I only knew that nobody near me had seen anything. I rang the police and said only what I could see: a crowd and a frightened shopkeeper. The van arrived, and an hour later the child's mother walked up with the child in her arms. She had been at the pharmacy next door. By then Bhaskar's glass door was cracked.

qa.q: Where was Aparna waiting when the voice note went round?
qa.a: Aparna was waiting at the bus stop across from Bhaskar's stationery shop.

qa.q: What was Bhaskar feeling, standing behind the counter with hands raised?
qa.a: Bhaskar was frightened and helpless, pale and unable to speak while a crowd he had never harmed shouted at him.

qa.q: What did Aparna do when unable to tell what was true?
qa.a: Aparna rang the police and said only what could be seen: a crowd and a frightened shopkeeper.

qa.q: What might that night have been like for Bhaskar afterwards, with the cracked glass door?
qa.a: Bhaskar probably felt shaken and hurt, since the crowd had believed a false story so fast, and the cracked door would be a reminder.

grounding: An elder recalls watching a rumour on phones turn a crowd against an innocent shopkeeper while verified facts arrived too late.

subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
Rain hammered the station roof and the night train was two hours late. On the crowded platform Eshaan's phone buzzed with a forwarded message: “A woman is carrying off someone's child from the waiting hall.” Below it was a photo of Ira, taken from behind, a sleeping girl on her shoulder.

Within minutes a ring of men had gathered. “Where are you taking her?” “Show us the ticket!” Ira clutched the child, eyes wide, trying to speak over the voices. Nobody had waited for facts.

Eshaan looked at the message again: no name, no sender, nothing checkable. Eshaan walked to the railway guard. “There's a crowd around a woman with a child. Please come.” The guard arrived and asked calmly whether someone could be called for the child. Ten minutes later a woman ran in, dripping wet. “That's my sister! She's been holding my daughter while I bought tickets.”

qa.q: What did the forwarded message claim?
qa.a: The message claimed a woman was carrying off someone's child from the waiting hall.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling, clutching the child with wide eyes?
qa.a: Ira was frightened and helpless, trying to speak while a ring of men shouted, and nobody waited for facts.

qa.q: What choice did Eshaan make instead of joining the crowd?
qa.a: Eshaan noticed the message had no name or sender and asked the railway guard to come, rather than confronting Ira.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ira when the woman ran in and said the child was her daughter?
qa.a: Ira likely felt huge relief but also shaken and humiliated, since strangers had accused Ira before checking anything.

grounding: An observer watches a rumour on a messaging app turn a station crowd against an innocent woman, and facts arrive after the outrage has begun.
